en.title: Physics: the whole course
en.short: What physics covers, how physics degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What physics is
sections.text:
Physics is the study of matter, energy, motion, forces, space and time. It looks for patterns that hold across many situations and expresses them as laws or models. A model is not a final truth. It has a domain where it works well and edges where it fails or needs a more general theory. Newtonian mechanics works well for everyday speeds and sizes. Special relativity is needed when speeds approach the speed of light. Quantum mechanics is needed at atomic and smaller scales.

Physics matters because it underpins engineering, medicine, materials, energy, communications and our picture of the universe. It also teaches a way of thinking: define the system, state the assumptions, use mathematics to make predictions, and test those predictions against experiment.

These summaries teach principles and problem-solving. They do not replace your lecturer, your laboratory manual or your institution’s regulations. Physical constants and data change as measurements improve, so use the values given in your current course materials.

sections.heading: How a physics degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria a BSc in physics commonly takes four years. Some universities offer applied physics or industrial physics. A master’s degree usually adds one to two years, and a doctorate several years. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland a BSc commonly takes three years and an integrated master’s such as MPhys four. In Scotland each commonly takes one year longer. In the United States a bachelor’s commonly takes four years. Check your own handbook for the exact pattern, credit load and award.

The early years usually build mathematics and basic physics: calculus, vectors, mechanics, waves, thermal physics, electricity and magnetism, and optics. Laboratory work runs alongside. Later years add core theory and options. Most programmes end with a project or dissertation. A master’s adds advanced courses and a research dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage starts with measurement, units and uncertainty. It then covers mathematical tools, kinematics and Newtonian mechanics, work, energy and momentum, rotational motion and gravitation, oscillations and waves, thermal physics, electrostatics and direct-current circuits, magnetism and electromagnetic induction, and geometrical and wave optics.

The core stage usually includes special relativity, mathematical methods for physics, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, electrodynamics and Maxwell’s equations, quantum mechanics I and II, statistical mechanics, solid state physics, atomic and molecular physics, nuclear and particle physics, astrophysics and cosmology, electronics and instrumentation, computational physics, experimental physics and data analysis, photonics and laser physics, and scientific communication, ethics and the final-year project.

At master’s level, common topics are advanced quantum mechanics, quantum field theory, condensed matter many-body physics, and research methods with a dissertation. Not every institution covers every topic in the same year, and some topics appear as options.

sections.heading: How to study physics
sections.text:
Physics is learned by solving problems and checking meaning. Read a short section, close the book, and write the main idea and the conditions under which it holds. Then solve problems without looking at the solution. Draw a diagram before you write equations. Write units on every line. Ask whether the answer is plausible. Test limiting cases, such as very small or very large values, and check dimensions.

Keep a laboratory notebook in ink. Record the date, what you did, the readings, the uncertainties and any corrections. Do not copy data. Learn the mathematics as you need it, but keep returning to the physical meaning. Study in short, active sessions and explain ideas aloud to a friend. Use past questions to find gaps, not to memorise answers.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The most common mistake is using a formula without its conditions. For example, constant-acceleration equations do not apply when acceleration changes. Other common errors are mixing units, making sign errors, treating vectors as scalars, and confusing mass with weight or heat with temperature.

Students also round too early, ignore uncertainty, and forget that an average value is not an instantaneous value. Some memorise derivations without understanding the assumptions. In the laboratory, some invent or smooth data, or leave out readings that do not fit. In computation, some trust software output without a hand check.

Write your assumptions clearly. An examiner needs to see how you reached the answer, not only the answer. If a result looks precise but unreasonable, stop and check the physics.

keyPoints: Physics studies matter, energy, motion, forces, space and time through models tested by experiment.
Degree length and awards vary by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course moves from measurement and mechanics to core theory, then to advanced master’s topics.
Solve problems actively, draw diagrams, write units on every line, and check limiting cases.
Use formulas only within their conditions, and keep uncertainties in laboratory work.
Write your assumptions clearly so that another person can follow and check your reasoning.

en.title: Measurement, units and uncertainty
en.short: SI units, dimensions, significant figures, errors, uncertainty propagation and graph plotting.

sections.heading: SI units and dimensions
sections.text: SI has seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Derived units are products of these, such as N = kg·m·s⁻². A dimension records the powers of mass M, length L, time T and so on. Dimensional analysis checks that every term in an equation has the same dimensions; it cannot fix dimensionless constants. It also converts units by multiplying by ratios equal to one.

sections.heading: Figures and errors
sections.text: Significant figures show the precision of a measurement. In multiplication and division, keep the smallest number of significant figures in the factors; in addition and subtraction, keep the smallest number of decimal places. Systematic error pushes readings in one direction, for example a zero error. Random error scatters readings; repeat and average to reduce it.

sections.heading: Uncertainty propagation
sections.text:
For independent random uncertainties, combine in quadrature. If y = a ± b then δy = √(δa² + δb²). If y = ab or a ÷ b then δy ÷ y = √((δa ÷ a)² + (δb ÷ b)²). For y = aⁿ, δy ÷ y = |n| δa ÷ a. A worst-case bound adds uncertainties directly instead.

Example: m = 12.0 ± 0.1 g and V = 5.0 ± 0.2 cm³. ρ = 12.0 ÷ 5.0 = 2.4 g/cm³. Fractional uncertainties are 0.1 ÷ 12.0 = 0.0083 and 0.2 ÷ 5.0 = 0.040. Combined: √(0.0083² + 0.040²) = 0.041. δρ = 2.4 × 0.041 = 0.098, so ρ = 2.4 ± 0.1 g/cm³.

sections.heading: Graphs and lab data
sections.text: Plot the independent variable on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis. Label each axis with quantity and unit, choose a scale that uses the paper, and add error bars. Draw a line of best fit; for a straight line find the gradient from two widely spaced points on the line. Linearise curves where possible, for example plot T² against length for a pendulum. Repeat readings, report the mean and its spread, and state every uncertainty.

keyPoints: SI has seven base units, and derived units come from them.
Dimensional analysis checks equations but cannot determine dimensionless constants.
Multiplication and division keep the least number of significant figures; addition and subtraction keep the least decimal places.
Systematic error shifts all readings one way; random error scatters them and is reduced by averaging.
For independent random uncertainties, δy = √(δa² + δb²) for sums and δy ÷ y = √((δa ÷ a)² + (δb ÷ b)²) for products or quotients.
Plot data with labelled axes and error bars, and use the line of best fit or a linearised graph.

en.title: Mathematical tools for physics
en.short: Algebra, trigonometry, vectors, calculus, complex numbers, series and first-order ODEs for physics.

sections.heading: Algebra and trigonometry
sections.text:
Physics problems start by naming quantities and writing equations that link them. Rearranging formulas, solving simultaneous equations and using logarithms are everyday algebra. Trigonometry resolves a vector into perpendicular components: a force F at angle θ to the x-axis has Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ. The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 often removes a variable.

Example: F = 5.0 N at 30°. Fx = 5.0 cos 30° = 4.33 N; Fy = 5.0 sin 30° = 2.50 N.

sections.heading: Vectors
sections.text: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. Add vectors by components: write each as (Ax, Ay), add the x parts and the y parts separately. If the resultant is R, it has magnitude √(Rx² + Ry²) and direction tan θ = Ry ÷ Rx. The scalar product A·B = AB cos θ gives work; the vector product A×B = AB sin θ gives torque, with direction from the right-hand rule.

sections.heading: Calculus and series
sections.text: The derivative is an instantaneous rate, such as v = dx/dt. The integral accumulates, such as x = ∫v dt. For small changes, series approximations simplify physics: (1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx for small x, and e^x ≈ 1 + x + x²/2. Always state the condition for the approximation.

sections.heading: Complex numbers and ODEs
sections.text: A complex number z = x + iy has modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) and argument θ = arctan(y/x). Euler’s formula e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ turns oscillations into exponentials. A first-order differential equation such as dy/dt = −ky has solution y = y0 e^(−kt); k is the decay constant. This models cooling, discharge and radioactive decay.

keyPoints: Resolve a vector with Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ; its magnitude is √(Fx² + Fy²).
The derivative gives an instantaneous rate of change, and the integral gives accumulated change.
For small x, (1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx and e^x ≈ 1 + x + x²/2.
Euler’s formula e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ links complex numbers to oscillations.
The first-order equation dy/dt = −ky has solution y = y0 e^(−kt).
After solving, check units, limiting cases and the condition for any approximation.

en.title: Kinematics and Newtonian mechanics
en.short: Displacement, velocity, acceleration, projectiles, circular motion, Newton’s laws and equilibrium.

sections.heading: Describing motion
sections.text: Displacement is change in position: a vector with magnitude and direction. Velocity is displacement ÷ time; speed is the scalar size of velocity. Acceleration is change in velocity ÷ time. For constant acceleration only, v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as. Choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent: slowing down means acceleration opposite to velocity.

sections.heading: Projectiles and circles
sections.text: Projectile motion separates horizontal and vertical motion. Ignoring air resistance, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is g downward. A ball launched at 20 m/s at 30° has horizontal component 20cos30 = 17.32 m/s and vertical 20sin30 = 10 m/s. With g = 9.8 m/s², flight time is 2×10÷9.8 = 2.04 s and range is 17.32×2.04 = 35.3 m. In uniform circular motion speed is constant but direction changes, giving centripetal acceleration a = v²/r toward the centre.

sections.heading: Newton’s laws
sections.text: Newton’s first law: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a resultant force acts. The second law: resultant force F = ma, in the same direction as the acceleration. The third law: if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force on a different body. A free-body diagram shows only the forces on one chosen object: weight, normal reaction, tension, friction and applied forces.

sections.heading: Friction and equilibrium
sections.text: Friction opposes relative sliding. Static friction adjusts up to a maximum μsN; kinetic friction is approximately μkN, where μ is the coefficient and N the normal force. A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of forces is zero, so ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. Example: a 5 kg block sliding on a horizontal floor with μk = 0.30 and a 20 N horizontal pull. Friction = 0.30×5×9.8 = 14.7 N; resultant = 20−14.7 = 5.3 N; acceleration = 5.3÷5 = 1.06 m/s².

keyPoints: Displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors; speed is the scalar size of velocity.
For constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as.
Projectile motion treats horizontal and vertical motion separately; horizontal velocity is constant if air resistance is ignored.
Uniform circular motion has centripetal acceleration a = v²/r directed toward the centre.
Newton’s second law is F = ma for the resultant force; third-law forces act on different bodies.
A particle is in equilibrium when ΣF = 0; friction has a maximum static value μsN and kinetic value about μkN.

en.title: Work, energy and momentum
en.short: Work, power, kinetic and potential energy, conservation, impulse, momentum, collisions and centre of mass.

sections.heading: Work and power
sections.text: Work is energy transferred by a force through a distance. For a constant force, W = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Work is a scalar in joules (J). Power is the rate of work: P = W ÷ t, or P = Fv cos θ. Its unit is the watt (W), 1 J/s. Example: a 10 N force pulls a 2 kg block 3 m at 60° to the motion. W = 10 × 3 × cos 60° = 15 J. From rest on a smooth floor, ½mv² = 15 J gives v = √(2 × 15 ÷ 2) = √15 ≈ 3.87 m/s. If this takes 5 s, average power is 3 W.

sections.heading: Energy
sections.text: Kinetic energy is energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Potential energy is stored energy from position or shape. Near Earth, gravitational PE = mgh for small height changes. A spring has elastic PE = ½kx², where k is the spring constant and x is extension. A conservative force does work independent of path and zero work around a closed loop. Gravity and spring forces are conservative; friction is not. If only conservative forces do work, KE + PE is conserved. With friction, mechanical energy falls, but total energy is conserved.

sections.heading: Momentum and impulse
sections.text: Linear momentum is p = mv, a vector along the velocity, in kg·m/s. Impulse is the change in momentum from a force acting for a time: J = FΔt = Δp. This is Newton’s second law in momentum form. If the net external force on a system is zero, total momentum is conserved. This applies to collisions and explosions.

sections.heading: Collisions and centre of mass
sections.text: In an elastic collision, momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not. In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and share one final velocity. The centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position: xcm = Σ(mi xi) ÷ Σmi. It moves as if all mass and external forces acted there.

keyPoints: Work done by a constant force is W = Fd cos θ, and power is P = W ÷ t = Fv cos θ.
Kinetic energy is ½mv²; gravitational potential energy near Earth is mgh and spring potential energy is ½kx².
A conservative force’s work is path-independent, and mechanical energy is conserved when only conservative forces do work.
Impulse equals change in momentum: J = FΔt = Δp, with p = mv.
Total momentum is conserved when net external force is zero; elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy.
The centre of mass is xcm = Σ(mi xi) ÷ Σmi and moves as if all mass were there.

en.title: Rotational motion and gravitation
en.short: Torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum, gravitation, Kepler’s laws and satellite orbits.

sections.heading: Torque and inertia
sections.text:
Torque τ is the turning effect of a force: τ = rF sin θ, where r is distance from pivot and θ is the angle between r and the force. Unit: newton metre. A rigid body resists angular acceleration with moment of inertia I, which depends on mass distribution about the axis. For a solid cylinder about its central axis, I = ½MR². Newton’s second law for rotation is τ = Iα.

Example: M = 2.0 kg, R = 0.50 m, τ = 3.0 N·m.
I = ½ × 2.0 × 0.50² = 0.25 kg·m².
α = 3.0 ÷ 0.25 = 12 rad/s².

sections.heading: Angular momentum
sections.text: Angular momentum L = Iω for a rigid body about a fixed axis, with ω in rad/s. If external torque is zero, L is conserved: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. A spinning skater speeds up by pulling in the arms. Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω². For rolling without slipping, v = ωR and total kinetic energy is ½Mv² + ½Iω².

sections.heading: Gravitation
sections.text: Newton’s law of gravitation states F = GMm/r², attractive along the line joining the centres. G is the gravitational constant. Gravitational potential at distance r from a spherical mass M is V = −GM/r, taking V = 0 at infinity. Potential energy of mass m is U = −GMm/r. The negative sign means a bound object needs energy to escape. Near Earth’s surface, ΔU ≈ mgh is an approximation.

sections.heading: Kepler and orbits
sections.text: Kepler’s laws: planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus; a line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times; T² is proportional to a³ for bodies orbiting the same central mass, where a is semi-major axis. For a circular satellite orbit, gravity supplies centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The period is T = 2πr/v, giving T² = 4π²r³/(GM). Here M is the central mass.

keyPoints: Torque is τ = rF sin θ and τ = Iα for rotation about a fixed axis.
For a solid cylinder about its axis, I = ½MR².
Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when external torque is zero.
Newton’s law of gravitation is F = GMm/r² and gravitational potential is V = −GM/r.
Kepler’s third law for orbits around the same central mass is T² ∝ a³.
For a circular satellite orbit, v = √(GM/r) and T = 2π√(r³/(GM)).

en.title: Oscillations and waves
en.short: Simple harmonic motion, damping, resonance, wave properties, superposition, standing waves and sound.

sections.heading: Simple harmonic motion
sections.text:
Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is motion under a restoring force proportional to displacement: F = −kx. Acceleration is a = −ω²x, where ω = 2πf = 2π/T. Speed is maximum at equilibrium (vmax = Aω); acceleration is maximum at the ends (amax = Aω²). Energy is constant: E = ½kA².

For a mass on a spring, T = 2π√(m/k); for a small-swing pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g).

Example: m = 0.50 kg, k = 50 N/m, A = 0.10 m. ω = √(50/0.50) = 10 rad/s, T = 0.628 s, vmax = 1.0 m/s, E = 0.25 J.

sections.heading: Damping and resonance
sections.text:
Damping is loss of oscillation energy, often to friction or air resistance. Light damping makes amplitude decay slowly. Critical damping returns to equilibrium fastest without overshooting. Heavy damping returns slowly without oscillation.

Resonance occurs when a driving frequency is near the natural frequency. Amplitude peaks, limited by damping. It explains tuning; unwanted resonance is reduced by damping or changing stiffness or mass.

sections.heading: Wave properties
sections.text:
A wave carries energy, not matter. Transverse waves disturb perpendicular to travel; longitudinal waves disturb parallel. Wavelength λ is the distance between adjacent points in phase; frequency f = 1/T. The wave equation is v = fλ.

For a stretched string, v = √(F/μ), where F is tension and μ is mass per unit length. Example: F = 40 N, μ = 0.010 kg/m gives v = √(4000) = 63.2 m/s.

sections.heading: Superposition, standing waves, sound
sections.text:
Superposition means overlapping wave displacements add. In-phase waves interfere constructively; opposite-phase waves interfere destructively. Similar frequencies produce beats at fbeat = |f1 − f2|.

A standing wave forms when identical waves travel in opposite directions, as on a string fixed at both ends. Nodes have zero motion; antinodes have maximum motion. Allowed wavelengths are λn = 2L/n and frequencies fn = nv/(2L).

Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave. Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude or intensity, and quality on the harmonic mix. Hearing spans about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, falling with age.

keyPoints: SHM: F = −kx, a = −ω²x, ω = 2πf = 2π/T, and E = ½kA².
Mass-spring period T = 2π√(m/k); small-swing pendulum period T = 2π√(L/g).
Damping removes oscillation energy; critical damping returns fastest without overshoot, and resonance peaks near natural frequency.
Wave equation v = fλ; on a stretched string v = √(F/μ).
Superposition adds displacements; beats have frequency |f1 − f2|.
Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends have λn = 2L/n and fn = nv/(2L); sound is a longitudinal pressure wave.

en.title: Thermal physics: heat, gases and the first law
en.short: Temperature, heat, expansion, calorimetry, ideal gases, the first law and entropy.

sections.heading: Temperature and heat
sections.text: Temperature measures how hot or cold a body is and sets the direction of heat flow. For an ideal gas, kelvin temperature is proportional to the mean translational kinetic energy of its molecules. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. Bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature. Specific heat capacity c is energy per kilogram per kelvin: Q = mcΔT. Latent heat L is energy per kilogram to change phase at constant temperature: Q = mL.

sections.heading: Expansion and calorimetry
sections.text: For a solid, length change is ΔL = αLΔT, where α is the linear expansivity. For a solid that expands equally in all directions, area and volume changes use about 2α and 3α. Calorimetry balances heat lost and gained in an insulated system. Example: heating 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 60 °C, with c = 4200 J/(kg·K), needs Q = 0.50 × 4200 × 40 = 84,000 J. A 100 W heater would take 840 s.

sections.heading: Ideal gases
sections.text: An ideal gas obeys pV = nRT, where n is the amount of substance in moles and R = 8.31 J/(mol·K); T must be in kelvin. Kinetic theory explains pressure as molecular collisions. The mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kT, so a monatomic ideal gas, one atom per molecule, has internal energy U = (3/2)nRT. Example: 1.0 mol at 300 K in 0.024 m³ has p = 1.0 × 8.31 × 300 ÷ 0.024 = 1.04 × 10⁵ Pa.

sections.heading: First law and entropy
sections.text: The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q − W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done by the system. For a gas at constant pressure, W = pΔV. Entropy S measures how spread out energy is. The second law says total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease in spontaneous changes. Heat flows from hot to cold, and no heat engine can convert all its heat input into work.

keyPoints: Temperature sets the direction of heat flow; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
Specific heat capacity gives Q = mcΔT, and latent heat gives Q = mL.
Thermal expansion: ΔL = αLΔT; area and volume changes use about 2α and 3α for a solid expanding equally in all directions.
Ideal gas law: pV = nRT, with T in kelvin and R = 8.31 J/(mol·K).
Kinetic theory gives mean translational kinetic energy (3/2)kT per molecule and U = (3/2)nRT for a monatomic ideal gas.
First law: ΔU = Q − W, where W is work done by the system; the second law says total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease in spontaneous changes.

en.title: Electrostatics and direct-current circuits
en.short: Charge, Coulomb’s law, field, potential, Gauss’s law, capacitance, current, Ohm’s law, Kirchhoff’s rules, RC circuits.

sections.heading: Charge and force
sections.text:
Electric charge is measured in coulombs (C) and is quantised in units of e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. Coulomb’s law gives the force between two point charges: F = k q₁ q₂ ÷ r², where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² and r is the separation.

Example: q₁ = 2.0 μC, q₂ = 3.0 μC, r = 0.10 m.
F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (0.10)²
= 8.99 × 10⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻¹² ÷ 0.010 = 5.4 N (repulsive).

sections.heading: Field and potential
sections.text: Electric field E is force per unit positive charge: E = F ÷ q. For a point charge Q, E = kQ ÷ r², directed away from positive Q. Electric potential V is energy per unit charge: V = kQ ÷ r, in volts (V). The field is the negative gradient of potential, E = −dV ÷ dr. A charge q moved through a potential difference ΔV changes energy by qΔV.

sections.heading: Gauss and capacitance
sections.text: Gauss’s law states that electric flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ε₀: Φ = ∮E·dA = Qenclosed ÷ ε₀, where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space. It gives E = Q ÷ (4πε₀r²) outside a spherical charge. A capacitor stores charge Q at voltage V, with C = Q ÷ V in farads (F). A parallel-plate capacitor has C = ε₀A ÷ d. Stored energy is ½CV².

sections.heading: Current and RC circuits
sections.text: Current I is charge flow rate, I = Q ÷ t, in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes current, with V = IR (Ohm’s law) for an ohmic conductor. Kirchhoff’s rules: the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero (current in equals current out), and the algebraic sum of voltage changes around a loop is zero. In an RC circuit the capacitor charges through a resistor with time constant τ = RC. After one τ it reaches about 63% of its final voltage; after five τ it is nearly complete.

keyPoints: Coulomb’s law: F = k q₁ q₂ ÷ r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Electric field E = F ÷ q and potential V = kQ ÷ r; E = −dV ÷ dr.
Gauss’s law: flux through a closed surface = enclosed charge ÷ ε₀.
Capacitance C = Q ÷ V; parallel plate C = ε₀A ÷ d; energy ½CV².
Ohm’s law V = IR; Kirchhoff’s junction and loop rules conserve charge and energy.
RC time constant τ = RC; after τ the capacitor reaches about 63% of final voltage.

en.title: Magnetism and electromagnetic induction
en.short: Magnetic forces, fields of currents, Faraday and Lenz laws, inductance and AC basics.

sections.heading: Magnetic forces
sections.text: A magnetic field B exerts force on moving charges and currents. The tesla (T) is one newton per ampere metre. Force on charge q at speed v, angle θ to B: F = qvB sinθ. On straight wire length L, current I: F = BIL sinθ. Use the right-hand rule: fingers along v or I, curl to B, thumb gives F for positive charge. Force is zero when motion is parallel to B.

sections.heading: Fields of currents
sections.text: Currents create magnetic fields. A long straight wire carrying I gives B = μ0 I ÷ (2πr) at distance r, where μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. The field circles the wire. Inside a long solenoid with n turns per metre, B = μ0 n I, nearly uniform along the axis. A coil is many turns; its field is the sum of its turns’ fields.

sections.heading: Induction laws
sections.text: Magnetic flux Φ = BA cosθ measures field through area A; θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area, and Φ is in webers (Wb). Faraday’s law: induced emf in N turns is ε = −N ΔΦ ÷ Δt. Lenz’s law explains the minus sign: induced current opposes the change. A rod length l moving at speed v across B has motional emf ε = Blv. Example: 100-turn coil, area 0.020 m², B perpendicular to the coil, rises from 0.10 T to 0.30 T in 0.50 s. ΔΦ = 0.20 × 0.020 = 0.0040 Wb. ε = 100 × 0.0040 ÷ 0.50 = 0.80 V.

sections.heading: Inductance and AC
sections.text: Self-inductance L, in henries (H), is flux linkage per ampere. It gives back emf ε = −L ΔI ÷ Δt. A coil stores energy U = ½LI². An AC generator rotates a coil in a magnetic field, giving sinusoidal emf V = V0 sin(2πft). The rms value Vrms = V0 ÷ √2 is the steady value giving the same power. Frequency f is cycles per second, in hertz (Hz).

keyPoints: Magnetic force on a charge is F = qvB sinθ; on a straight wire it is F = BIL sinθ.
A long straight wire gives B = μ0 I ÷ (2πr); a long solenoid gives B = μ0 n I.
Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cosθ, and Faraday’s law is ε = −N ΔΦ ÷ Δt.
Lenz’s law says the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux.
Self-inductance gives ε = −L ΔI ÷ Δt and stored energy U = ½LI².
For sinusoidal AC, Vrms = V0 ÷ √2 and frequency f is measured in hertz.

en.title: Geometrical and wave optics
en.short: Reflection, refraction, lenses, instruments, interference, diffraction and polarisation.

sections.heading: Reflection and refraction
sections.text:
At a surface, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction obeys Snell’s law, n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2, where n = c ÷ v is the refractive index. From denser to less dense, total internal reflection starts beyond the critical angle, sin θc = n2 ÷ n1.

Example: air (n = 1.00) to glass (n = 1.50) at 30°: sin θ2 = (1.00 ÷ 1.50) sin 30° = 0.333, so θ2 = 19.5°. Glass to air gives θc = 41.8°.

sections.heading: Lenses and instruments
sections.text:
A thin lens obeys 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ v + 1 ÷ u (real-is-positive convention), with magnification m = v ÷ u. Converging lenses have positive f, diverging lenses negative f. Instruments such as the eye, camera, magnifying glass, microscope and telescope combine lenses. A microscope uses a short-focus objective and an eyepiece; a telescope uses a long-focus objective.

Example: f = 10 cm, u = 30 cm. 1 ÷ v = 1 ÷ 10 − 1 ÷ 30 = 2 ÷ 30, so v = 15 cm. m = 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5: a real, inverted image half the object size.

sections.heading: Interference and diffraction
sections.text:
Wave superposition explains interference and diffraction. Coherent sources keep constant phase difference. Young’s double slit gives bright fringes at path difference mλ and dark fringes at (m + ½)λ; spacing is Δy = λD ÷ d. Single-slit minima: a sin θ = mλ, m = 1, 2, ...; a grating gives maxima at d sin θ = mλ.

Example: λ = 600 nm, d = 0.20 mm, D = 2.0 m. Δy = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0) ÷ (0.20 × 10⁻³) = 6.0 mm.

sections.heading: Polarisation
sections.text: Light is transverse; its electric field can be polarised. A polariser halves unpolarised intensity. Malus’s law gives I = I0 cos² θ for a second polariser at θ. Brewster’s angle, tan θB = n2 ÷ n1, gives complete polarisation on reflection.

keyPoints: The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
Snell’s law is n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2, and total internal reflection begins at sin θc = n2 ÷ n1 when n1 > n2.
For a thin lens, 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ v + 1 ÷ u in the real-is-positive convention, with m = v ÷ u; sign conventions vary between textbooks.
Young’s double slit has fringe spacing Δy = λD ÷ d, and a diffraction grating has maxima at d sin θ = mλ.
Malus’s law is I = I0 cos² θ, and Brewster’s angle satisfies tan θB = n2 ÷ n1.
Interference and diffraction need coherent sources, and polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave.

en.title: Special relativity
en.short: Einstein’s postulates, Lorentz transformations, simultaneity, time dilation, length contraction and relativistic energy.

sections.heading: Postulates
sections.text:
An inertial frame is one in which a free body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity.

Einstein’s first postulate says the laws of physics have the same form in every inertial frame. The second says light in vacuum travels at c in every inertial frame, whatever the motion of the source or observer. Together they link space and time, and they make c a universal speed limit.

sections.heading: Lorentz transformations
sections.text:
Let frame S' move at speed v along the x axis of frame S. The Lorentz factor is γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − v²/c²).

The Lorentz transformations are x' = γ(x − vt) and t' = γ(t − vx/c²); the inverse swaps the sign of v. They preserve the spacetime interval s² = c²t² − x². When v is much less than c, γ is close to 1 and they reduce to the Galilean x' = x − vt and t' = t.

sections.heading: Clocks and rulers
sections.text:
Two events simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another if they are separated along the direction of relative motion. This is relativity of simultaneity.

A clock at rest in a frame measures proper time τ; moving observers measure Δt = γτ, so moving clocks run slow. A rod at rest has proper length L0; moving observers measure L = L0 ÷ γ along the motion. Transverse lengths are unchanged. These effects are reciprocal: each observer sees the other’s clock slow and the other’s rod shortened.

sections.heading: Momentum and energy
sections.text:
Relativistic momentum is p = γmv. Total energy is E = γmc², rest energy is E0 = mc², and kinetic energy is K = (γ − 1)mc². These give E² = p²c² + m²c⁴. Mass is a form of energy; a change in energy ΔE changes mass by Δm = ΔE ÷ c².

Example: v = 0.6c gives γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − 0.36) = 1.25. For proper time 2.0 μs, Δt = 2.5 μs; for proper length 10 m, L = 8.0 m. For m = 1.0 kg, p = 1.25 × 1.0 × 0.6c = 2.25 × 10⁸ kg m/s, E = 1.125 × 10¹⁷ J, K = 2.25 × 10¹⁶ J.

keyPoints: Einstein’s postulates: physics is the same in all inertial frames, and light in vacuum has speed c in all of them.
Lorentz factor: γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − v²/c²); x' = γ(x − vt) and t' = γ(t − vx/c²).
Moving clocks run slow: Δt = γτ, where τ is proper time.
Moving rods shorten along the motion: L = L0 ÷ γ, where L0 is proper length.
Relativistic momentum and energy: p = γmv, E = γmc², K = (γ − 1)mc², and E² = p²c² + m²c⁴.
Mass and energy are equivalent: rest energy E0 = mc², and ΔE = Δm c².

en.title: Mathematical methods for physics
en.short: Vector calculus, complex analysis, Fourier methods, differential equations, special functions and Green functions.

sections.heading: Vector calculus
sections.text:
Vector calculus extends calculus to fields. The gradient gives the direction of steepest increase of a scalar field. Divergence measures source strength, and curl measures rotation.

The divergence theorem and Stokes theorem turn volume or surface integrals into boundary integrals. They are used in electromagnetism and fluid flow.

sections.heading: Complex analysis and Fourier methods
sections.text:
Complex analysis studies functions of z = x + iy, where i² = −1. A function is analytic where it has a derivative in the complex sense. Cauchy’s theorem says the integral of an analytic function around a closed path is zero. The residue theorem evaluates contour integrals: the integral equals 2πi times the sum of the enclosed residues, and this is used to compute real integrals.

Fourier series write a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines. Fourier transforms do the same for non-periodic functions, replacing the sum by an integral. They turn differentiation into multiplication and convolution into products, so linear systems are easier to solve.

sections.heading: Differential equations and Green functions
sections.text:
Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) involve one independent variable; partial differential equations (PDEs) involve several. Linear ODEs with constant coefficients are solved by characteristic equations, and first-order linear ODEs by integrating factors. PDEs such as Laplace, heat and wave equations are solved by separation of variables, which reduces them to ODEs. Boundary conditions select allowed solutions and eigenvalues.

A Green function solves a linear equation with a source: if L G(x,x') = δ(x − x'), then u(x) = ∫ G(x,x') f(x') dx' solves L u = f. Green functions are used in electrostatics, quantum scattering and diffusion.

sections.heading: Special functions and example
sections.text:
Special functions arise from separation of variables: Bessel functions in cylindrical problems, Legendre polynomials in spherical problems, and Hermite functions in the harmonic oscillator.

Example: the Fourier sine series of f(x) = x on −π < x < π is 2 Σ (−1)^(n+1) sin(nx) ÷ n. At x = π/2 the first term is 2 sin(π/2) = 2, while the exact value is π/2 ≈ 1.571; more terms improve the estimate.

keyPoints: Gradient, divergence and curl describe scalar and vector fields; the divergence theorem and Stokes theorem relate integrals to boundaries.
Cauchy’s theorem says integrals of analytic functions around closed paths are zero; the residue theorem evaluates contour integrals, with residues used to compute real integrals.
Fourier series represent periodic functions; Fourier transforms represent non-periodic functions and convert differentiation to multiplication.
Separation of variables reduces linear PDEs such as Laplace, heat and wave equations to ODEs.
A Green function satisfies L G(x,x') = δ(x − x') and gives u(x) = ∫ G(x,x') f(x') dx' for L u = f.
Bessel, Legendre and Hermite functions are standard special functions from cylindrical, spherical and oscillator problems.

en.title: Classical mechanics: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian methods
en.short: Constraints, Lagrange and Hamilton equations, Poisson brackets, central forces and small oscillations.

sections.heading: Generalised coordinates
sections.text: A constraint is a restriction on motion, such as a bead on a wire. A holonomic constraint can be written as a relation between coordinates and time, so it removes degrees of freedom. Choose independent generalised coordinates q_i, one per degree of freedom, instead of Cartesian coordinates plus constraint forces. For N particles without constraints there are 3N coordinates; each independent holonomic constraint removes one. Velocities are q̇_i = dq_i/dt.

sections.heading: Lagrange equations
sections.text: For conservative systems define L = T − V, the Lagrangian, with T kinetic and V potential energy. The Euler-Lagrange equations are d/dt(∂L/∂q̇_i) − ∂L/∂q_i = 0. They follow from Hamilton’s principle, that the action ∫L dt is stationary. Non-conservative generalised forces Q_i are added on the right as Q_i. These equations are equivalent to Newton’s laws for the chosen coordinates. Example: a mass m on a spring k has L = ½mẋ² − ½kx², giving mẍ + kx = 0.

sections.heading: Hamilton and brackets
sections.text: Define p_i = ∂L/∂q̇_i and H = Σ p_i q̇_i − L. For standard conservative systems H = T + V. Hamilton’s equations are q̇_i = ∂H/∂p_i and ṗ_i = −∂H/∂q_i. The Poisson bracket is {f,g} = Σ(∂f/∂q_i ∂g/∂p_i − ∂f/∂p_i ∂g/∂q_i). Then df/dt = ∂f/∂t + {f,H}; a quantity with no explicit time dependence is conserved when {f,H} = 0.

sections.heading: Central forces and oscillations
sections.text: In a central force V depends only on r, so angular momentum J is conserved. Write U_eff = V(r) + J²/(2mr²); stable circular orbits occur at its minimum. For small oscillations about stable equilibrium, expand V to second order. Normal modes are independent sinusoidal motions. Example: m = 0.50 kg, k = 8.0 N/m gives ω = √(k/m) = √16 = 4.0 rad/s and T = 2π/ω = 1.57 s.

keyPoints: Generalised coordinates q_i are independent coordinates, one per degree of freedom; holonomic constraints reduce their number.
Lagrange’s equations: d/dt(∂L/∂q̇_i) − ∂L/∂q_i = 0, with L = T − V for conservative systems.
Hamilton’s equations: q̇_i = ∂H/∂p_i and ṗ_i = −∂H/∂q_i, with p_i = ∂L/∂q̇_i.
Poisson bracket: {f,g} = Σ(∂f/∂q_i ∂g/∂p_i − ∂f/∂p_i ∂g/∂q_i), and df/dt = ∂f/∂t + {f,H}.
Central-force motion conserves angular momentum J and uses U_eff = V(r) + J²/(2mr²).
Small oscillations about stable equilibrium are found by expanding V to second order; for a mass on a spring, ω = √(k/m).

en.title: Electrodynamics and Maxwell’s equations
en.short: This summary covers Maxwell’s equations in vacuum and matter, potentials, gauges, waves, radiation and boundary conditions.

sections.heading: Field equations
sections.text:
In vacuum Maxwell’s equations are ∇·E = 0, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t and ∇×B = (1/c²)∂E/∂t. A changing field drives the other; c = 1/√(μ0ε0).

In matter, free charge density ρf and free current density Jf appear: ∇·D = ρf, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, ∇×H = Jf + ∂D/∂t. D = ε0E + P and H = B/μ0 − M, with P polarisation and M magnetisation. The ∂D/∂t term is the displacement current.

sections.heading: Potentials and gauge
sections.text:
Because ∇·B = 0, B = ∇×A for a vector potential A. Then ∇×E = −∂B/∂t gives E = −∇V − ∂A/∂t, with V the scalar potential. A and V are not unique: adding ∇χ to A and subtracting ∂χ/∂t from V leaves E and B unchanged. This is gauge invariance.

A common choice is the Lorenz gauge, ∇·A + (1/c²)∂V/∂t = 0, which makes the wave equations for A and V symmetric. The Coulomb gauge, ∇·A = 0, is useful in atomic physics.

sections.heading: Waves and radiation
sections.text:
In vacuum the fields obey ∇²E − (1/c²)∂²E/∂t² = 0, and for B. Plane waves are transverse: E and B are perpendicular to the direction of travel and to each other, with E = cB. In a linear medium the speed is v = 1/√(με) and the refractive index n = c/v.

A charge with acceleration a radiates power P = q²a²/(6πε0c³), the Larmor formula. Retarded potentials show that the field depends on the source a time r/c earlier. Example: μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m and ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m give c = 1/√(μ0ε0) = 2.998×10⁸ m/s.

sections.heading: Boundary conditions
sections.text: At an interface, the normal component of B is continuous and the normal component of D jumps by the free surface charge density σf: D1n − D2n = σf. The tangential component of E is continuous. The tangential component of H jumps by the free surface current density Kf. They follow from the integral forms applied to a pillbox or loop.

keyPoints: In vacuum Maxwell’s equations are ∇·E = 0, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t and ∇×B = (1/c²)∂E/∂t.
In matter ∇·D = ρf, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t and ∇×H = Jf + ∂D/∂t.
Potentials give B = ∇×A and E = −∇V − ∂A/∂t, and gauge changes leave the fields unchanged.
The Lorenz gauge ∇·A + (1/c²)∂V/∂t = 0 gives symmetric wave equations for A and V.
Plane waves in vacuum travel at c = 1/√(μ0ε0), with E perpendicular to B and E = cB.
At a boundary Bn is continuous, Dn jumps by σf, Et is continuous and Ht jumps by Kf.

en.title: Quantum mechanics I: wavefunctions, wells and tunnelling
en.short: Wave-particle duality, the wavefunction, Schrödinger equation, square well, oscillator and tunnelling.

sections.heading: Wave-particle duality
sections.text: Light and matter show both wave and particle behaviour. In the photoelectric effect, light delivers energy in packets of energy E = hf, where h is Planck’s constant and f is frequency. In electron diffraction, electrons produce interference patterns, yet they arrive as single hits. The de Broglie relation p = h/λ links momentum p to wavelength λ. These are complementary descriptions, not a contradiction.

sections.heading: Wavefunction and probability
sections.text: The wavefunction ψ(x,t) is a complex function that encodes what can be known about a particle. The probability of finding it in a small interval dx is |ψ|² dx, where |ψ|² = ψ*ψ is the probability density. The wavefunction must be normalised so that ∫|ψ|² dx = 1 over all space. Measurement outcomes are probabilistic; ψ does not say where the particle is before measurement.

sections.heading: Schrödinger equation and well
sections.text: The Schrödinger equation governs how ψ evolves. The time-independent form in one dimension is −(ħ²/2m)d²ψ/dx² + V(x)ψ = Eψ, where ħ = h/(2π), m is mass, V is potential energy and E is total energy. For an infinite square well of width L, ψ = 0 at the walls and E_n = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²), n = 1,2,3,... Example: an electron in L = 1 nm has E1 ≈ 0.376 eV. Check: E1 = π²(1.055×10⁻³⁴)² ÷ [2(9.11×10⁻³¹)(10⁻⁹)²] = 6.02×10⁻²⁰ J ≈ 0.376 eV.

sections.heading: Oscillator and tunnelling
sections.text: The harmonic oscillator has potential V = ½mω²x², where ω is the angular frequency, and equally spaced levels E_n = (n + ½)ħω, n = 0,1,2,... The lowest energy is not zero; this zero-point energy follows from the uncertainty principle. Quantum tunnelling is the chance of crossing a barrier even when E < V. For a rectangular barrier of width L, with κ = √[2m(V−E)]/ħ, the transmission probability falls roughly as T ≈ exp(−2κL) when κL is large. This explains alpha decay and scanning tunnelling microscopy.

keyPoints: Wave-particle duality: E = hf and p = h/λ.
The probability density is |ψ|², and the wavefunction is normalised so ∫|ψ|² dx = 1.
Time-independent Schrödinger equation: −(ħ²/2m)d²ψ/dx² + Vψ = Eψ.
Infinite square well: E_n = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²), n = 1,2,3,...
Harmonic oscillator: E_n = (n + ½)ħω, with zero-point energy ½ħω.
Tunnelling transmission falls approximately as exp(−2κL), where κ = √[2m(V−E)]/ħ.

en.title: Quantum mechanics II: atoms, spin and approximation methods
en.short: Covers angular momentum, hydrogen, spin, identical particles, perturbation theory, variational method and scattering.

sections.heading: Angular momentum and hydrogen
sections.text:
Angular momentum in quantum mechanics is quantised. For orbital motion, L² has eigenvalues l(l+1)(h/2π)² and Lz has m(h/2π), with l = 0, 1, 2, ... and m = −l, ..., +l. Spherical harmonics Ylm are the eigenfunctions.

The hydrogen atom has a Coulomb potential V = −e²/(4π ε0 r). Its bound-state energies are E_n = −13.6 eV ÷ n², ignoring reduced-mass and relativistic corrections. Each n has n² degenerate orbitals before spin; radial functions R_nl and Ylm give shape.

Example: the 2 to 1 transition has photon energy 13.6 − 3.4 = 10.2 eV. Using hc = 1240 eV nm, λ = 1240 ÷ 10.2 = 121.6 nm.

sections.heading: Spin and identical particles
sections.text:
Spin is an intrinsic angular momentum with no classical analogue. An electron has s = 1/2, so S² = s(s+1)(h/2π)² and Sz = ms(h/2π) with ms = ±1/2. Spin is not orbital motion.

Identical particles obey quantum statistics. Fermions, such as electrons, have half-integer spin and a total wavefunction antisymmetric under exchange; this gives the Pauli exclusion principle. Bosons have integer spin and a symmetric wavefunction. In helium, the two electrons must have an antisymmetric total wavefunction.

sections.heading: Perturbation and variational methods
sections.text:
Time-independent perturbation theory treats a small extra potential V added to a solved Hamiltonian H0. The first-order energy shift is ΔE_n = <n|V|n>. The first-order state correction mixes other states, with denominator E_n − E_k; the formula fails if levels are degenerate. Second-order shifts are usually smaller.

The variational method guesses a trial wavefunction ψ and computes E[ψ] = <ψ|H|ψ> ÷ <ψ|ψ>. For the ground state, E[ψ] is always at or above the true energy E0. Minimising E with respect to trial parameters gives an upper bound.

sections.heading: Scattering
sections.text: Scattering experiments measure a differential cross-section dσ/dΩ, the scattered rate per unit solid angle divided by the incident flux. For a weak potential, the Born approximation gives the scattering amplitude as a Fourier transform of V(r). The total cross-section is the integral of dσ/dΩ over all directions. Partial-wave methods are better at low energy.

keyPoints: Orbital angular momentum is quantised: L² = l(l+1)(h/2π)² and Lz = m(h/2π), with l = 0, 1, 2, ... and m = −l, ..., +l.
Hydrogen bound-state energies are E_n = −13.6 eV ÷ n² in the simple nonrelativistic model, with n² degenerate orbitals before spin.
An electron has spin s = 1/2, with Sz = ±(h/2π)/2, and fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle.
First-order perturbation energy shift: ΔE_n = <n|V|n>.
The variational ground-state energy E[ψ] = <ψ|H|ψ> ÷ <ψ|ψ> is an upper bound to E0.
The Born approximation expresses the scattering amplitude as a Fourier transform of the potential; dσ/dΩ is the differential cross-section.

en.title: Statistical mechanics: ensembles, partition functions and phase transitions
en.short: Ensembles, partition functions, ideal Fermi and Bose gases, and phase transitions.

sections.heading: Ensembles and partition function
sections.text:
An ensemble is many copies of a system in different microscopic states. The microcanonical ensemble describes an isolated system with fixed N, V and energy E; its entropy is S = k_B ln Ω, where Ω counts accessible states. The canonical ensemble has fixed N, V and temperature T, in contact with a heat bath. A state of energy E has probability proportional to exp(−E/k_BT), and the partition function is Z = Σ exp(−E/k_BT). The Helmholtz free energy is F = −k_BT ln Z. The grand canonical ensemble fixes the chemical potential μ, V and T and allows particle exchange; μ is the energy change when one particle is added. Its grand partition function is Ξ = Σ exp[−(E − μN)/k_BT]. Derivatives give averages.

Example: two levels 0 and ε have Z = 1 + exp(−ε/k_BT). For ε = 0.1 eV at 300 K, k_BT = 0.0259 eV, exp(−ε/k_BT) = 0.0209, and mean energy = 0.1 × 0.0209 ÷ 1.0209 = 0.00205 eV.

sections.heading: Ideal quantum gases
sections.text: Ideal quantum gases use the same grand canonical framework. Fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so each state holds at most one particle. The mean occupation is f = 1 ÷ [exp((ε − μ)/k_BT) + 1]. At T = 0 fermions fill states up to the Fermi energy. Bosons may share a state, with f = 1 ÷ [exp((ε − μ)/k_BT) − 1]. For a free Bose gas μ ≤ 0. Below a critical temperature the ground state becomes macroscopically occupied: Bose-Einstein condensation. At high T and low density both gases approach the classical Boltzmann result.

sections.heading: Phase transitions
sections.text: Phase transitions occur when the free energy becomes non-analytic in the thermodynamic limit. A first-order transition has latent heat and a jump in the order parameter, such as magnetisation. A continuous transition has no latent heat but a diverging correlation length. Mean-field theory replaces interactions by an average field and gives approximate critical exponents. Near the critical point fluctuations matter, and the renormalisation group explains universality: different microscopic models share the same exponents.

keyPoints: Microcanonical: fixed N, V, E, with S = k_B ln Ω.
Canonical: fixed N, V, T, with Z = Σ exp(−E/k_BT) and F = −k_BT ln Z.
Grand canonical: fixed chemical potential μ, V, T, with Ξ = Σ exp[−(E − μN)/k_BT].
Fermi occupation is 1 ÷ [exp((ε − μ)/k_BT) + 1]; Bose occupation is 1 ÷ [exp((ε − μ)/k_BT) − 1].
Bose-Einstein condensation is macroscopic occupation of the ground state below a critical temperature.
Phase transitions appear as non-analytic free energy; mean-field theory gives approximate exponents, while the renormalisation group explains universality.

en.title: Solid state physics: crystals, diffraction, phonons and bands
en.short: Crystal lattices, reciprocal space, X-ray diffraction, phonons, free electrons, bands and semiconductors.

sections.heading: Crystal lattices
sections.text: A crystal is a periodic array of atoms. The lattice is the set of points; the basis is the atom or group placed at each point. The repeat unit is the unit cell, described by three lattice vectors a, b, c. The reciprocal lattice is the set of wavevectors G for which plane waves have the periodicity of the lattice. Its unit cell is the first Brillouin zone, the space in which electron and phonon wavevectors are drawn. A simple cubic lattice with spacing a has reciprocal spacing 2π/a.

sections.heading: X-ray diffraction
sections.text: X-rays of wavelength λ scatter from parallel planes spaced d. They add in phase when Bragg’s law holds: nλ = 2d sinθ, where θ is measured from the plane and n is an integer. The structure factor tells which reflections are strong or absent because of the basis. Example: λ = 0.150 nm, d = 0.250 nm, n = 1. Then sinθ = 0.150 ÷ (2 × 0.250) = 0.300, so θ = 17.5°.

sections.heading: Phonons and electrons
sections.text: Atoms vibrate about lattice sites. The normal modes are quantised as phonons, with energy hν. Their dispersion ω(k) gives acoustic modes (sound) and, with more than one atom per cell, optical modes. The free-electron model ignores the lattice potential: electrons fill states up to the Fermi energy EF, and only electrons near EF respond. The density of states g(E) counts states per energy interval.

sections.heading: Bands and semiconductors
sections.text: Band theory adds the periodic potential. Bloch’s theorem makes electron states extend through the crystal, and allowed energies form bands separated by gaps. Metals have a partly filled band; insulators and semiconductors have a filled valence band and an empty conduction band. In a semiconductor the gap is small enough for thermal excitation. Holes behave as positive carriers, and effective mass m* describes response to forces. Doping with donors or acceptors adds electrons or holes and shifts the Fermi level.

keyPoints: Bragg’s law is nλ = 2d sinθ for diffraction from planes spaced d.
For a simple cubic lattice of spacing a, the reciprocal lattice spacing is 2π/a, and the first Brillouin zone is its Wigner-Seitz cell.
Phonons are quantised lattice vibrations with energy hν; acoustic modes have zero frequency at long wavelength.
In the free-electron model, electrons fill states up to the Fermi energy EF at zero temperature.
Band theory explains metals, insulators and semiconductors through band filling and band gaps.
In semiconductors, a small band gap allows thermal excitation, and doping with donors or acceptors controls electron and hole concentrations.

en.title: Atomic and molecular physics
en.short: Multi-electron atoms, fine and hyperfine structure, selection rules, molecular bonding and spectra.

sections.heading: Multi-electron atoms
sections.text: In a multi-electron atom each electron moves in the average field of the nucleus and the other electrons. Screening lowers the nuclear charge to an effective charge Z_eff, so outer electrons are less tightly bound. The Pauli principle allows at most two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins. Configurations fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, and Hund’s rules give the lowest term for a partly filled subshell. Light atoms use LS coupling, combining L and S into J; heavy atoms need jj coupling.

sections.heading: Fine and hyperfine
sections.text: Fine structure splits a level through spin-orbit coupling, the interaction of electron spin with orbital motion, plus relativistic and Darwin corrections. It grows with Z. Hyperfine structure is much smaller and comes from the nuclear magnetic moment interacting with the electrons; it depends on nuclear spin I. The hydrogen 21 cm line is a hyperfine transition between the two ground-state spin arrangements.

sections.heading: Selection rules
sections.text: Electric dipole transitions obey Δl = ±1 and Δm_l = 0, ±1. In LS coupling they also require ΔS = 0, ΔL = 0, ±1 and ΔJ = 0, ±1, but J = 0 to J = 0 is forbidden; parity must change. These rules explain the discrete lines of atomic spectra and why some levels are metastable. Line positions are term differences; fine and hyperfine splitting gives closely spaced components.

sections.heading: Molecular spectra
sections.text: Molecular bonding uses the Born-Oppenheimer approximation: heavy nuclei move slowly, so electronic and nuclear motions separate. Linear combination of atomic orbitals gives bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals; bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) ÷ 2. Rotational levels have E_J = J(J+1)ℏ² ÷ (2I), giving frequency lines spaced by 2B, where B = h ÷ (8π²I). Vibrational levels are E_v = (v + 1/2)hν, with Δv = ±1 in the harmonic model. Example: I = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴⁶ kg m² gives B = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ ÷ (8π² × 2.0 × 10⁻⁴⁶) = 4.20 × 10¹⁰ Hz, so B ÷ c ≈ 1.40 cm⁻¹ and spacing ≈ 2.80 cm⁻¹.

keyPoints: Electron configurations follow the Pauli principle, increasing orbital energy and Hund’s rules.
Fine structure comes from spin-orbit and relativistic corrections; hyperfine structure comes from nuclear spin.
Electric dipole selection rules are Δl = ±1, Δm_l = 0, ±1, with ΔS = 0, ΔL = 0, ±1, ΔJ = 0, ±1 (not 0 to 0) and a parity change.
Molecular orbitals give bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) ÷ 2.
Rotational energies are E_J = J(J+1)ℏ² ÷ (2I), with line spacing 2B and B = h ÷ (8π²I).
Vibrational energies are E_v = (v + 1/2)hν, with Δv = ±1 in the harmonic model.

en.title: Nuclear and particle physics
en.short: Binding energy, radioactive decay, fission and fusion, then quarks, leptons and the Standard Model.

sections.heading: Nucleus and binding energy
sections.text:
A nuclide has mass number A (protons plus neutrons) and atomic number Z (protons). Isotopes share Z but differ in A. A nucleus weighs less than its separate nucleons; this mass defect gives binding energy E = Δm c². Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron, so fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy.

Helium-4, with 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²:
Δm = 2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) − 4.002603 = 0.030377 u
BE = 0.030377 × 931.5 = 28.30 MeV, so BE/A = 7.07 MeV.

sections.heading: Radioactive decay
sections.text:
Decay is random, so the number of nuclei left is N = N₀ e^(−λt), where λ is the decay constant. Half-life T½ = ln2 ÷ λ. Activity A = λN is measured in becquerels (Bq), one decay per second. Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus, beta decay changes a neutron into a proton or the reverse, and gamma emission removes excess energy.

Example: T½ = 10 days, so after 30 days three half-lives pass and the fraction left is (1/2)³ = 0.125, that is 12.5%.

sections.heading: Fission, fusion and reactions
sections.text: Nuclear reactions conserve charge Z, mass number A, energy and momentum. The Q value is the mass change times c². Fission splits a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235, releasing about 200 MeV and neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction. Fusion joins light nuclei; D + T → He-4 + n releases about 17.6 MeV but needs very high temperature to overcome Coulomb repulsion.

sections.heading: Elementary particles
sections.text: Matter particles are quarks and leptons, each in six flavours across three generations. Quarks form hadrons: baryons such as the proton (uud) and mesons such as pions (quark plus antiquark). Leptons include the electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos. Forces are carried by gauge bosons: photon for electromagnetism, W and Z for the weak force, gluon for the strong force. The Higgs boson explains particle masses. The Standard Model does not include gravity.

keyPoints: Mass defect gives binding energy E = Δm c²; binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron.
Decay follows N = N₀ e^(−λt), with T½ = ln2 ÷ λ and activity A = λN.
Fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy; D + T → He-4 + n gives about 17.6 MeV.
Nuclear reactions conserve Z, A, energy and momentum; Q is the mass change times c².
Quarks and leptons are matter particles; gauge bosons carry the forces, and the Standard Model excludes gravity.

en.title: Astrophysics and cosmology
en.short: Stars, the HR diagram, galaxies, the expanding universe, dark matter, dark energy and the Big Bang.

sections.heading: Stars and HR diagram
sections.text: A star is held against gravity by pressure from hot gas and radiation. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium and releases energy. The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram plots luminosity (intrinsic brightness) against surface temperature; most stars lie on the main sequence, where they fuse hydrogen. After the main sequence, a star expands into a red giant. Its final fate depends on mass: a low-mass star leaves a white dwarf, a heavier one a neutron star, and the heaviest collapse to a black hole.

sections.heading: Galaxies and dark matter
sections.text: Galaxies are gravitationally bound systems of stars, gas and dust. They are classed as spiral, elliptical or irregular. Spiral galaxies rotate too fast for their visible mass to hold them together, so they must contain dark matter: matter that does not emit or absorb light. Gravitational lensing and the motions of galaxies in clusters give further evidence.

sections.heading: The expanding universe
sections.text: Hubble’s law states that a galaxy’s recession speed is v = H₀d, where H₀ is the Hubble constant. Distant galaxies show redshifted light, meaning stretched to longer wavelengths, and the cosmic microwave background is relic radiation from a hot, dense early universe. These support the Big Bang model. The expansion is accelerating, which is attributed to dark energy, a poorly understood component. Dark matter and dark energy together are inferred to make up most of the universe’s mass-energy, but their nature is unknown.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc. A galaxy at d = 100 Mpc recedes at v = 70 × 100 = 7,000 km/s. The Hubble time is 1/H₀ = (3.086 × 10¹⁹ km/Mpc) ÷ (70 km/s) = 4.41 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14.0 Gyr, a rough age estimate for the universe.

keyPoints: Stars are powered by nuclear fusion and held up by pressure; their mass sets their evolution and final remnant.
The HR diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature, and most stars lie on the main sequence.
Galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing and cluster motions are evidence for dark matter.
Hubble’s law is v = H₀d; redshift and the cosmic microwave background support the Big Bang.
The expansion is accelerating, which is attributed to dark energy.
The Hubble time 1/H₀ gives a rough age of the universe, about 14 Gyr for H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc.

en.title: Electronics and instrumentation
en.short: Diodes, transistors, op amps, digital logic, sensors, noise, signal conditioning and measurement.

sections.heading: Diodes and transistors
sections.text: A diode is a pn junction that conducts mainly one way. In forward bias a silicon diode drops about 0.6 to 0.7 V; this varies with current and temperature. It rectifies alternating current and protects circuits. A transistor is a three-terminal device that controls current. In a bipolar junction transistor the base current controls collector current, with IC ≈ βIB. A field-effect transistor uses gate voltage instead. Transistors work as switches or amplifiers. In digital circuits they switch between cut-off and saturation.

sections.heading: Operational amplifiers
sections.text: An operational amplifier is a high-gain differential amplifier. With negative feedback its two inputs sit at nearly the same voltage, and almost no current enters them. The non-inverting amplifier has gain G = 1 + Rf ÷ R1. Example: Rf = 90 kΩ, R1 = 10 kΩ, so G = 10. An input of 0.25 V gives 2.5 V output. Op amps also buffer, filter, integrate and compare signals.

sections.heading: Digital logic
sections.text: Digital logic represents information as two voltage levels, high and low, called 1 and 0. Gates such as AND, OR and NOT combine bits according to Boolean rules. Combinational logic has no memory; sequential logic uses flip-flops and a clock. Logic families differ in speed, power and voltage levels, so check compatibility.

sections.heading: Sensors and measurement
sections.text: A sensor, or transducer, converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal. Examples are a thermocouple for temperature, a strain gauge for force and a photodiode for light. The signal is often small, so signal conditioning amplifies it, filters unwanted frequencies and lowers impedance. Noise is random unwanted fluctuation. Thermal noise in a resistor has rms voltage √(4kTRB), where k is Boltzmann’s constant, T is absolute temperature, R is resistance and B is bandwidth. Measurement needs calibration against a known standard. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability. Loading and poor grounding cause errors.

keyPoints: Silicon diodes conduct mainly in forward bias and drop about 0.6 to 0.7 V, a value that varies with current and temperature.
Transistor current gain is IC ≈ βIB for a bipolar junction transistor; FETs are controlled by gate voltage.
With negative feedback an ideal op amp has a virtual short between its inputs; non-inverting gain is G = 1 + Rf ÷ R1.
Digital logic uses gates and Boolean rules; sequential circuits add memory through flip-flops and a clock.
Sensors convert physical quantities to electrical signals, and signal conditioning amplifies, filters and buffers them.
Thermal noise rms voltage is √(4kTRB); calibration, accuracy, precision and loading all affect measurement quality.

en.title: Computational physics: numerical methods and simulation
en.short: Numerical integration, root finding, ODE and PDE solvers, Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, fitting and error.

sections.heading: Error and integration
sections.text:
Numerical error has two main parts. Truncation error comes from replacing an exact process by a finite formula, such as a sum over sampled points. Round-off error comes from finite floating-point precision. A smaller step usually reduces truncation error but can increase round-off and cost. A method converges if its error tends to zero as the step shrinks; it is stable if small errors do not grow.

Numerical integration estimates an integral from sampled values. The trapezium rule with n equal strips of width h gives ∫f dx ≈ h[f0/2 + f1 + ... + fn−1 + fn/2]. Example: f(x)=x² on [0,1], n=2, h=0.5. Values are 0, 0.25, 1, so T = 0.5(0 + 2×0.25 + 1)/2 = 0.375. Exact value 1/3 = 0.333..., error 0.0417.

sections.heading: Roots and ODEs
sections.text:
Root finding solves f(x)=0. Bisection brackets a sign change and halves the interval, giving linear convergence. Newton-Raphson uses x_{n+1}=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n) and converges quadratically near a simple root. For √2, start x0=1: x1=1.5, x2=1.4167.

Ordinary differential equation (ODE) solvers advance y'=f(t,y). Euler uses y_{n+1}=y_n+h f(t_n,y_n), first order. Runge-Kutta fourth order (RK4) combines four slope estimates for fourth-order accuracy. Step size controls accuracy, cost and stability.

sections.heading: Monte Carlo and MD
sections.text:
Monte Carlo methods use random samples. To estimate an integral, average f over N random points in the region and multiply by the region’s volume. Statistical error falls as about 1/√N, slowly, but the method works in high dimensions.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulates atoms by computing forces from a potential and integrating Newton’s equations with a small timestep. A thermostat controls temperature, and the timestep must resolve the fastest vibration.

sections.heading: Fitting and PDEs
sections.text:
Data fitting chooses parameters to minimise residuals, often by least squares: χ²=Σ[(y_i−model_i)/σ_i]². Good fitting also checks residuals and uncertainties, not only the best curve.

Partial differential equations (PDEs) are often solved by finite differences on a grid. Explicit schemes can be unstable unless a condition such as the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) limit is met. Refine the grid to test convergence.

keyPoints: Truncation and round-off errors limit numerical accuracy; convergence and stability must be checked.
The trapezium rule is ∫f dx ≈ h[f0/2 + f1 + ... + fn−1 + fn/2].
Newton-Raphson uses x_{n+1}=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n) and converges quadratically near a simple root.
Euler is first order and RK4 is fourth order for ODEs.
Monte Carlo error scales as about 1/√N, and MD integrates Newton’s equations with a small timestep.
Least squares minimises χ²=Σ[(y_i−model_i)/σ_i]², while PDE finite differences need stability and grid refinement.

en.title: Experimental physics and data analysis
en.short: Advanced laboratory practice, detectors, counting statistics, uncertainty propagation, curve fitting and reporting.

sections.heading: Instruments and detectors
sections.text:
An instrument is characterised by sensitivity (response per unit input), resolution (smallest resolvable change), linearity (constant sensitivity over the range) and calibration against a traceable standard. Detectors add efficiency (fraction of events detected), dead time (time after a pulse when the detector cannot respond) and background (signal without the source).

A counting measurement with N counts has Poisson uncertainty σ_N = √N, so the relative uncertainty is 1/√N. For N = 400, σ_N = 20 counts, 5% relative uncertainty. Repeat runs and background runs separate signal from noise.

sections.heading: Statistics of measurements
sections.text:
Random errors scatter; systematic errors shift readings. For repeated readings, report the mean x̄ = Σx_i/n and the sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x_i − x̄)²/(n − 1)]. The standard error of the mean is s/√n.

Type A uncertainties come from repeated data; Type B from calibration certificates, manufacturer limits or judgement. Combine independent contributions in quadrature: σ_total = √(σ_A² + σ_B²).

sections.heading: Uncertainty and fitting
sections.text:
For independent x_i and y = f(x_i), propagate uncertainties with σ_y² = Σ(∂f/∂x_i)² σ_i². For a product or quotient, relative uncertainties add in quadrature.

Example: R = V/I with V = 12.0 ± 0.1 V and I = 2.00 ± 0.02 A. R = 6.00 Ω. Relative uncertainties: 0.1/12 = 0.0083 and 0.02/2 = 0.010. σ_R/R = √(0.0083² + 0.010²) = 0.013, so σ_R = 0.08 Ω. Report R = 6.00 ± 0.08 Ω.

Least-squares fitting minimises Σ(y_i − mx_i − c)²; inspect residuals (data minus fit). When the uncertainties differ, weight the fit with the chi-square statistic χ² = Σ[(y_i − f(x_i))²/σ_i²], where σ_i is the uncertainty of each point (for Poisson counts, σ_i² is the expected count).

sections.heading: Reporting results
sections.text:
Record raw data, calibration, settings and analysis in a notebook so another person can repeat the work. State the result as value ± uncertainty with units, giving the uncertainty to one or two significant figures and matching the value.

Label graph axes with units, show error bars and a residual plot. Explain rejected data and systematic checks. A report separates method, results, uncertainty budget (a list of each uncertainty contribution and its size) and conclusion.

keyPoints: Calibrate every instrument against a traceable standard and record sensitivity, resolution, linearity, efficiency, dead time and background.
For N counts, the Poisson uncertainty is σ_N = √N and the relative uncertainty is 1/√N.
For repeated readings, the mean is x̄ = Σx_i/n, the sample standard deviation is s = √[Σ(x_i − x̄)²/(n − 1)] and the standard error of the mean is s/√n.
Combine independent uncertainties in quadrature; for y = f(x_i), σ_y² = Σ(∂f/∂x_i)² σ_i².
Least-squares fitting minimises Σ(y_i − mx_i − c)², and residuals and chi-square χ² = Σ[(y_i − f(x_i))²/σ_i²] test the fit.
Report value ± uncertainty with units, give uncertainty to one or two significant figures and match the value, and keep a repeatable record.

en.title: Photonics and laser physics
en.short: Light coherence, laser action, optical fibres and waveguides, and nonlinear optical effects.

sections.heading: Light and coherence
sections.text:
Photonics uses light in science and technology. In a medium of refractive index n, light travels at v = c ÷ n, where c is the vacuum speed. Its wavevector is k = nω ÷ c. Coherence measures phase predictability.

Temporal coherence means the phase stays correlated over a delay; coherence time τc is roughly 1 ÷ Δν, where Δν is the source linewidth, and coherence length is Lc ≈ c τc ÷ n. Spatial coherence means a fixed phase relation across the beam. Lasers are highly coherent; lamps are not.

sections.heading: Lasers and waveguides
sections.text:
A laser has a gain medium, a pump and an optical resonator. Pumping creates population inversion: more atoms or molecules are in the upper laser level than the lower one. A photon then stimulates emission of an identical photon, with the same frequency, phase, direction and polarisation. The resonator selects modes and returns light for more amplification. Lasing starts when gain exceeds loss. For a linear cavity of length L, mirror reflectivities R1 and R2, and distributed loss α, threshold gain is g = α + [1 ÷ (2L)] ln[1 ÷ (R1R2)].

An optical fibre guides light by total internal reflection. In a step-index fibre, core index n1 exceeds cladding index n2. The numerical aperture in air is NA = √(n1² − n2²), and acceptance angle θa = arcsin(NA). A waveguide confines a mode; single-mode operation needs a small core and normalised frequency V below 2.405.

Example: n1 = 1.48 and n2 = 1.46.
NA = √(1.48² − 1.46²) = √(2.1904 − 2.1316) = √0.0588 = 0.2425
θa = arcsin(0.2425) ≈ 14.0°

sections.heading: Nonlinear optics
sections.text:
Nonlinear optics appears at high intensity. The polarisation is P = ε0(χ⁽¹⁾E + χ⁽²⁾E² + χ⁽³⁾E³ + ...).

The χ⁽²⁾ term causes second harmonic generation and frequency mixing, but only in media lacking inversion symmetry. The χ⁽³⁾ term gives the Kerr effect, n = n0 + n2I, and four-wave mixing. Efficient processes need phase matching.

keyPoints: In a medium of refractive index n, light travels at v = c ÷ n and has wavevector k = nω ÷ c.
Coherence time is roughly 1 ÷ Δν and coherence length is Lc ≈ c τc ÷ n.
Laser action needs population inversion, stimulated emission and gain above loss; threshold gain is g = α + [1 ÷ (2L)] ln[1 ÷ (R1R2)].
An optical fibre guides light by total internal reflection; numerical aperture is NA = √(n1² − n2²) and acceptance angle is arcsin(NA).
Single-mode step-index fibre operation needs normalised frequency V below about 2.405.
Nonlinear effects come from χ⁽²⁾ and χ⁽³⁾ terms; second harmonic generation needs a non-centrosymmetric medium and phase matching.

en.title: Scientific communication, ethics and the final-year project
en.short: Searching literature, writing and presenting physics, research ethics and planning a final-year project.

sections.heading: Finding literature
sections.text: Start with a clear question and a list of keywords, including synonyms and symbols. Use Boolean operators: AND narrows, OR widens, NOT excludes. Search a general index such as Google Scholar and subject databases your library provides; check each source’s date, author and peer-review status. Primary sources report original work; reviews summarise a field. Record every reference in a reference manager and keep a log of your searches, so you can cite consistently.

sections.heading: Writing and speaking
sections.text: Scientific writing is concise and verifiable. A physics report usually has title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. State what you did, what you found and what it means; give units and uncertainties. Figures need labelled axes and captions. In a talk, one idea per slide, large text, and rehearse to time. Explain the question, method, result and limitation, then invite questions.

sections.heading: Ethics and plagiarism
sections.text: Research ethics means honesty in producing and reporting data, and care for the welfare and safety of anyone affected by the work. Fabrication invents data; falsification alters or selects data misleadingly. Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s words, ideas, figures or code as your own without attribution. Self-plagiarism reuses your own published work without saying so. Cite sources, quote sparingly, and follow your institution’s rules. Authorship needs a real contribution. Get permission for images and follow safety or ethics approval where required.

sections.heading: Project planning
sections.text: Plan with your supervisor: define scope, milestones, risks and a realistic timetable. Keep a dated lab notebook and back up data. Meet regularly and write as you go. Case: Amina plans a final-year project on solar-cell efficiency. She searches, drafts a question, books equipment, keeps a notebook and writes monthly progress notes. When a reading is anomalous she records it and repeats the measurement rather than deleting it. She cites all sources and presents uncertainties. Her report follows the department’s format and she checks it against the marking guide.

keyPoints: Use keywords, synonyms and Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) to search literature, and record sources in a reference manager.
Scientific writing states method, results and interpretation concisely, with units, uncertainties and labelled figures.
Plagiarism is using another person’s words, ideas, figures or code without attribution; fabrication and falsification are separate serious offences.
Plan the final-year project with your supervisor, setting scope, milestones, risks and a timetable.
Keep dated records, back up data and report anomalous results honestly rather than deleting them.
Follow your department’s report format and referencing style, and rehearse presentations to time.

en.title: Advanced quantum mechanics
en.short: Path integrals, second quantisation, scattering theory, density matrices and open systems.

sections.heading: Path integrals
sections.text: The path-integral amplitude from x to y in time T is a sum over all paths of exp(iS/ħ), where S is the action evaluated along that path. The classical path dominates when S ≫ ħ because other paths cancel by phase. Gaussian path integrals give the free-particle propagator. The method extends to fields and makes symmetry and topology visible.

sections.heading: Second quantisation
sections.text: Second quantisation treats particle number as an observable. States live in Fock space and are labelled by occupation numbers. Creation and annihilation operators add or remove a particle. Bosons obey [a_i, a_j†] = δ_ij; fermions obey anticommutation rules, which enforce the Pauli principle. Field operators ψ(x) combine these modes with spatial wavefunctions.

sections.heading: Scattering theory
sections.text:
The S-matrix maps incoming asymptotic states to outgoing ones; its non-trivial part is the T-matrix. Cross-sections follow from |T|² with phase-space factors. For spinless elastic scattering, partial-wave analysis gives σ = (4π/k²) Σ (2l+1) sin² δ_l, where δ_l is the phase shift and k the wave number. The Born approximation treats the potential as a weak perturbation.

Example: if only l=0 contributes, δ_0 = π/2 and k = 1 fm^-1, then σ = 4π ÷ (1 fm^-1)² = 4π fm² ≈ 12.6 fm².

sections.heading: Density matrix
sections.text:
A density matrix ρ = Σ p_i |ψ_i><ψ_i| describes a statistical mixture. Tr ρ = 1 and <A> = Tr(ρA). A pure state has Tr ρ² = 1; a mixed state has Tr ρ² < 1. Tracing out an environment gives a reduced density matrix and decoherence. Open-system dynamics is often written with the Lindblad equation, which adds dissipative terms to unitary evolution.

Example: ρ = diag(0.7, 0.3) gives Tr ρ² = 0.49 + 0.09 = 0.58, so the state is mixed.

keyPoints: The path integral sums exp(iS/ħ) over paths; the classical path dominates when S ≫ ħ.
Second quantisation uses creation and annihilation operators on Fock space; bosons commute and fermions anticommute.
The S-matrix gives scattering amplitudes; cross-sections follow from |T|² and phase space.
For spinless elastic scattering, σ = (4π/k²) Σ (2l+1) sin² δ_l.
The density matrix gives probabilities and expectation values: Tr ρ = 1 and <A> = Tr(ρA).
A pure state has Tr ρ² = 1; a mixed state has Tr ρ² < 1, and the Lindblad equation describes open-system evolution.

en.title: Quantum field theory
en.short: Canonical field quantisation, Feynman diagrams, gauge theories, renormalisation and the Standard Model.

sections.heading: Fields and quantisation
sections.text: In quantum field theory a field φ(x) is defined at every point of space and time. Canonical quantisation promotes it to an operator. For a real scalar field, impose [φ(x), π(y)] = iδ³(x − y) at equal times, where π is the conjugate momentum. Expand φ in plane waves with annihilation a(k) and creation a†(k′) operators, with [a(k), a†(k′)] = (2π)³ δ³(k − k′). The quanta of the field are particles. For fermions, use anticommutators instead.

sections.heading: Feynman diagrams
